raw_case_text:
A 71-year-old male patient from Sur de Bolivar, Colombia, with no known medical history, was admitted to the hospital from a lower level of care with a one-day history of psychomotor agitation and incoherent speech. Extra-institutional laboratory tests showed moderate anemia of normal volume and severe thrombocytopenia with a thick positive smear for P. vivax. Due to the neurological involvement, they suspected complicated malaria and referred the patient to a higher level of care for management in the intensive care unit (ICU).
On admission to our institution, the patient was neurologically disoriented and somnolent without signs of meningeal irritation or focalization. The remaining physical examinations did not reveal any alterations. A simple brain scan revealed no pathological findings. Laboratory tests revealed elevated blood urea nitrogen, severe anemia with markers of non-autoimmune hemolysis, and schistocytes in the peripheral blood associated with severe thrombocytopenia. The thick control smear was negative. (Table 1). Complicated malarial syndrome was considered to be due to cerebral and hematological involvement, the latter suggestive of thrombotic microangiopathy secondary to the infectious process. The patient was admitted to the ICU, and treatment with intravenous artemisinin derivatives was initiated as first-line management for complicated malaria according to the Colombian guidelines, as well as supportive transfusion management.
Despite completing treatment with artesunate, the patient continued to have neurological, renal, and hematological abnormalities, with high transfusion requirements (Table 2). Therefore, given the persistence of laboratory findings with a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia profile (Table 2, day-3) and a PLASMIC score with a high probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, probable acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was considered, starting management with plasma exchange and high-dose steroids prior to recording ADAMTS13 levels.
After the initiation of therapeutic apheresis therapy and high-dose steroids, the patient showed substantial improvement in neurological symptoms, renal function, and hemolysis profile (Table 2, Day 7). The diagnosis of TTP was confirmed with a report of <0.1% ADAMTS13. Therefore, immunosuppression for relapse prevention was associated with rituximab. The patient received a total of (18 plasma exchanges and three doses of rituximab) (Table 2, day 15), achieving normalization of the platelet count, improvement and stability of hemoglobin, normalization of the hemolysis profile and renal injury, and clinically without neurological abnormalities, therefore, he was discharged from the hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old male from Sur de Bolivar, Colombia, presented with a 1-day history of psychomotor agitation and incoherent speech.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute psychomotor agitation and incoherent speech 1 day prior to admission. Initial extra-institutional testing showed normocytic moderate anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, and a positive thick smear for Plasmodium vivax, prompting ICU referral for suspected complicated cerebral malaria.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known past medical history; from Sur de Bolivar, Colombia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for psychomotor agitation, disorientation, somnolence, and incoherent speech.

objective.physical_examination: Neurologically disoriented and somnolent on admission, without signs of meningeal irritation or focal neurological deficits. Remaining systemic physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Extra-institutional labs showed normocytic moderate anemia and severe thrombocytopenia. Admission and Day 3 labs showed severe non-autoimmune microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with peripheral blood schistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia, elevated BUN/renal injury, and high PLASMIC score.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast brain CT scan revealed no pathological findings.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) triggered by or associated with Plasmodium vivax malaria. Extra-institutional thick blood smear was positive for P. vivax (admission repeat thick smear negative), and TTP was confirmed by severely deficient ADAMTS13 activity (<0.1%). Initially treated in the ICU with IV artesunate and blood transfusions; due to persistent microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, renal injury, and neurological dysfunction after completing artesunate, therapeutic plasma exchange (18 sessions total), high-dose corticosteroids, and rituximab (3 doses) were administered, achieving complete neurological, hematological, and renal recovery prior to discharge.
